narration: SKYSHIFT is Project Mercury Team's public application for traceable inspection of the infrared sky. This screen based walkthrough uses actual application screenshots and measured diagnostics, with computer generated narration. The release contains real Sphere X data. Scientific approval and independent human technical review remain pending.

Our current comparison focuses on a small region around the nucleus of M one oh one. The two observations were acquired on December seventh and December eleventh, twenty twenty five, in UTC. Both are real quick release two, detector two observations. The prepared north up grid has twenty four by twenty four pixels. Common usable coverage is ninety four point four four percent.

Registration is measured independently in the native images using Gaia reference positions propagated to each observation. No corrective transform is fitted to force agreement. Thirteen references lie inside the declared context and cover all four quadrants. The median measured residual is zero point three one arcseconds. The ninety fifth percentile is two point zero one arcseconds. These are sample residuals, not absolute precision or a motion detection limit.

Wavelength compatibility is checked across every common supported pixel. The maximum diagnostic is about zero point two four seven against the unchanged threshold of zero point two five. This does not prove identical response functions. Image sharpness and backgrounds also differ. The application supports qualitative inspection and questions for review. It does not confirm motion, brightness variability, calibrated subtraction, or a discovery.

This is the deployed browser interface. Side by side views share the same sky geometry, intensity scale, zoom, and pan. A and B switching preserves that viewport. Optional blinking starts only when requested, and reduced motion preferences are respected. Dates, wavelength information, unsupported pixels, and review status remain visible. The interface also adapts to narrow screens.

A visitor can add a note by selecting an image location or entering sky coordinates. Notes can be edited, located, or removed. Only coordinates within common valid support are allowed. The note shown here is explicitly a quality assurance demonstration, with no astronomical finding asserted. Notes stay in the current browser tab until the user exports the comparison.

The complete review packet preserves original images, full calibration, Gaia inputs, diagnostics, masks, and reproduction source. Compact exports preserve the prepared data, notes, exact settings, source references, hashes, and a preview. Sixty one Python tests and twenty three JavaScript tests pass. In a fresh environment, all ten prepared arrays reconstruct exactly. Production export and reopening, corruption rejection, and the full packet download have been verified.

The public software workflow is working. The remaining gates require real people: an independent team member must document the technical review, a qualified astronomical reviewer must assess scientific defensibility, and five novice sessions must evaluate usability. Synthetic scenes remain labeled test controls. Future discoveries and advanced analysis are not claimed. Every scientific approval stays pending until the necessary assessment is actually completed and documented.
